rewritten_text:
Raymond paced the room in anger. I stood prepared to hear his accusations and answer them. Adrian rested against the wall. “This is utterly absurd,” he exclaimed. “Schoolboys could scarcely behave with less reason.”

“You do not comprehend,” Raymond said. “This is but one part of a system, a plan of tyranny I shall never endure. Because I am England's Protector, must I be the one slave within her empire? Must my privacy be violated, my conduct condemned, my friends affronted? I will cast off the whole of it. Witness what I do!” He removed the star of office from his breast and flung it upon the table. “I resign my office and surrender my power. Let whoever wishes take it!”

“Let him take it,” cried Adrian, “who dares declare himself your superior, or whom the world will acknowledge as such. No man in England possesses presumption enough. Understand yourself, Raymond, and your anger will vanish; your satisfaction will return. A few months since, whenever we prayed for our country's prosperity or our own, we also prayed for the Protector's life and welfare, inseparably bound to both. You spent your hours for our advantage; your ambition sought our praise. You adorned our cities with buildings, supplied useful institutions, and enriched the earth with abundant fertility. The mighty and unjust trembled before your judgment-seat; the poor and oppressed lifted themselves like flowers waking at dawn beneath the sunshine of your care.

“Can you be surprised that we stand horrified and sorrowful when all this seems altered? Come, this fit of ill-humour has already ended. Take up your duties again. Your followers will acclaim you, your adversaries fall silent, and our love, honour, and allegiance will once more be shown. Govern yourself, Raymond, and the world will obey you.”

“These words would be excellent sense if spoken to another,” Raymond answered gloomily. “Study the lesson yourself, and you, the foremost peer of the realm, may become its ruler. Good, wise, and just as you are, you may command every heart. But I discover, too early for my own happiness and too late for England's welfare, that I accepted a task beyond my powers. I cannot govern myself. My passions rule me; the slightest impulse is my tyrant. Do you suppose I surrendered the Protectorate—and surrendered it I have—in a moment of peevishness? By the living God, I swear never to pick up that bauble again, never again to load myself with the cares and misery of which it is the outward emblem.

“Yes, it is—and I could have got it if I'd been big enough. I spotted him first. Who caught him?”

“An old man, a stranger. He sold his chance in him for forty dollars, because he's bound upriver and can't stay. Just think of that! I'd wait, you bet, if it took seven years.”

“So would I, every time,” I says. “But perhaps the chance ain't worth any more, if he's willing to sell so cheap. Maybe something about it ain't right.”

“It is right, though, straight as can be. I read the handbill myself. It describes him exact, like a picture, and names the plantation he come from below New Orleans. No, sir, there ain't any risk to that speculation, you can count on it. Say, got a chew of tobacco for me?”

I hadn't any, so he went away. I returned to the raft and sat in the wigwam trying to think. But I couldn't arrive at a thing. I thought till my head ached, and still couldn't find any way out. After such a long journey, and after everything we'd done for those rascals, it had all come to nothing. The whole business was wrecked, because they had the heart to play that trick on Jim and turn him into a slave for the rest of his life, among strangers besides, for forty miserable dollars.

Once I thought it would be a thousand times better for Jim to be a slave back home with his family, if a slave he had to be. I'd write Tom Sawyer, then, and have him tell Miss Watson where Jim was. But I soon dropped that idea for two reasons. She'd be furious and disgusted with his wickedness and ingratitude in leaving her, and would sell him right downriver again. Even if she didn't, everybody naturally hates an ungrateful nigger; they'd keep reminding Jim of it and make him feel mean and disgraced. And what about me! Word would spread everywhere that Huck Finn had helped a nigger win his freedom. If I ever met anybody from that town again, I'd be ashamed enough to kneel and lick his boots. That's how it goes: a fellow does something low, then doesn't want to bear what comes of it. He imagines there's no disgrace provided he keeps it hidden. That was exactly my situation. The longer I turned it over, the harder my conscience ground away at me, till I felt wickeder and lower and meaner all the time.

“I swear,” he cried, “by the sun, by the blue heavens, and by the fire of love burning in my heart, that if you grant my request, you will never see me again for as long as they endure. Go home and begin your work. I will follow its progress with anxiety beyond words, and you can be certain that I will appear when you are ready.”

With that he suddenly left, perhaps afraid I might change my mind. I watched him race down the mountain faster than an eagle could fly, until he quickly disappeared among the ridges of the sea of ice.

His story had taken the entire day, and the sun was on the horizon when he went. I knew I should hurry down towards the valley before darkness surrounded me, but my heart was heavy and my steps slow. Finding my way along the narrow mountain paths and keeping a firm footing bewildered me, absorbed as I was in the emotions the day's events had awakened. It was late at night when I reached the halfway resting place and sat beside the fountain. Stars appeared at intervals as clouds moved away from them. Dark pines rose before me, with a broken tree lying here and there on the ground. The scene had an extraordinary solemnity that stirred strange thoughts. I wept bitterly and clasped my hands in anguish. “Oh, stars and clouds and winds,” I cried, “you are all about to mock me. If you truly pity me, destroy my feelings and my memory. Let me become nothing. Otherwise, go away, go away, and leave me in darkness.”

These were wild, miserable thoughts. Yet I cannot tell you how heavily the stars' endless twinkling pressed upon me, or how I heard every gust of wind as though it were a dull, vicious sirocco coming to consume me.

Dawn had broken before I reached the village of Chamounix. Without resting, I set out immediately for Geneva. Even within my own heart, I could find no expression for my feelings. They bore down like a mountain, their immense weight crushing the very agony beneath them. In that state I returned home and went inside to face my family. My haggard, distraught appearance alarmed them deeply, but I answered none of their questions and barely spoke. I felt as though I were under a curse, as though I had no right to their sympathy, as though I could never again enjoy their companionship.
